Culture · Anime · Shibuya

A baby hitman disappeared from TV. His “family” never left.

Sixteen years after its last regular episode, Katekyo Hitman REBORN! has brought its old official festival back to Tokyo. The event is small enough to fit inside Shibuya Cast—and large enough to reveal how anime memory survives.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 17, 2026 · 17:40 JST · 7 min read
20years203 TV episodes

At Shibuya Cast today, a festival name from the late 2000s appeared again: Vongola Festa. The official Katekyo Hitman REBORN! event ran annually from 2007 through 2012, returned in 2017 and 2018, and then went quiet. For the television anime’s 20th anniversary, it is back for two days.

The event runs from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Saturday, October 17, and from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Sunday at Shibuya Cast’s Space and Garden areas. Admission is free, although entry to the indoor area required advance lottery registration. The program combines archive displays, mini-games, an event shop and a themed cafe. On Sunday, 50 lottery-selected guests can attend a birthday program with voice actors including Neeko, Yukari Kokubun, Hidekazu Ichinose and Suguru Inoue.

Those details describe a fan event. They do not explain why it matters. The unusual fact is that the television series stopped broadcasting new regular episodes in 2010. A generation later, its organizers can still revive a festival format, fill it with remembered voices and sell the idea of returning to a fictional “family.”

The joke that turned into a battle epic

Akira Amano’s manga began serialization in Shueisha’s Weekly Shonen Jump in 2004 and eventually filled 42 collected volumes. Its first premise is deliberately absurd: Tsunayoshi “Tsuna” Sawada is an unsuccessful middle-school student told that he is an heir to the Vongola Mafia family. His tutor is Reborn, a baby-sized professional hitman whose special bullet can make Tsuna face life with desperate resolve.

The opening material behaves like an episodic school comedy. Characters, weapons and rules arrive as punch lines. Then the structure changes. Rival groups, succession conflicts and a future timeline transform the series into a long-running battle narrative. That tonal migration is one reason the work remains easy to remember: viewers did not simply watch the cast grow stronger; they watched the genre itself expand around them.

The TV Tokyo anime began in October 2006 and ran to 203 episodes. The anniversary project has made that number part of its identity, releasing short selections from all 203 installments through official social channels. An official 20th-anniversary promotional film brings the cast and the series’ distinctive flame imagery back into motion without announcing a new TV season.

Official 20th-anniversary promotional video from the anime’s verified YouTube channel. This is official series footage, not a fan recreation. Watch on the official anime channel ↗

Why revive the festival rather than only the show?

Vongola Festa turns memory into a place. Streaming can make old episodes available, but it cannot reproduce the social experience around a long weekly broadcast: character songs, opening themes, voice-actor events, merchandise and the gradual discovery of a large ensemble. A physical festival rebuilds that surrounding world for a weekend.

The timing also connects several layers of the franchise. October is the anime’s anniversary month. The October 18 birthday program references both Reborn and Tsuna. The official campaign has already included a 203-episode scene project, an August popularity vote, September’s “REBORN! Music Month,” a Namja Town collaboration and a planned stage at Jump Festa 2027. The Shibuya event is therefore not an isolated nostalgia market; it is the physical midpoint of a year-long anniversary plan.

But the core reveal is what the organizers have not announced. The anniversary PV is not confirmation of a reboot, sequel or adaptation of later manga arcs. The official material celebrates the existing anime. That distinction matters because anniversary campaigns routinely generate expectations larger than their stated news. Today’s confirmed event is a festival revival, not a new television production.

A 2000s series in a different anime world

When REBORN! began airing, weekly television was the center of anime discovery, overseas simulcasts were limited, and fans often encountered long series unevenly. In 2026, a franchise can address viewers directly through YouTube shorts, music playlists and globally visible social accounts. The anniversary uses current distribution tools to reconstruct an older viewing rhythm one famous scene at a time.

That makes the work useful beyond fandom. It shows how Japanese media franchises preserve value between new adaptations. A completed manga does not become culturally inactive. Publishers, animation committees, venues, performers and fans can reactivate different parts of its history: a song one month, a favorite episode the next, then a shop or live event.

The event’s “family” language is especially effective because it mirrors the story. Tsuna’s Vongola circle is assembled from classmates, rivals and outsiders who become loyal through shared trials. Long-term viewers formed their own social circles around favorite guardians, pairings, openings and arcs. Reviving Vongola Festa asks them to return not merely as customers but as members of a group that still recognizes its symbols.

What a newcomer should notice

A first-time viewer should watch for the hinge between comedy and battle story. The early setup may feel loose because it is constructing a crowded cast and a vocabulary of dying-will bullets, rings and flames. Later conflicts reassign emotional weight to those comic inventions. The series’ visual appeal comes from that escalation: school uniforms and domestic jokes gradually coexist with elaborate weapons, sharply coded flame colors and formal Mafia succession imagery.

The official anniversary film is the safest visual starting point. Shueisha’s first-volume page provides the original manga premise, while the anime site separates confirmed anniversary projects from fan speculation. Together they show the difference between the property’s published history and the new activity happening today.

Vongola Festa closes Sunday afternoon. That is a brief return for a series with 203 episodes, 42 manga volumes and two decades of accumulated attachment. Yet the small scale is the point. The anime did not need to be on television every week for sixteen years to remain present. Its audience carried the family forward—and today, in Shibuya, the official event finally gave that memory a room again.
